note: Opened dl/ik_75521991.txt (Indian Kanoon, 2025 INSC 1288, Criminal Appeal No. 2195 of 2025, 6 November 2025, Gavai CJI with Masih J.). Paras 56 (i) to (iv) and the last sentence of para 58 ('this procedure as affirmed above shall govern arrests henceforth') are verbatim. The SCC citation (2026) 1 SCC 500 is footnote 1 of Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol (dl/ik_144049703.txt, line 379), and the same judgment, para 24, refers to 'the conclusions summarized in paragraph 66' and to 'paragraph 65' for the remand route, which confirms that the SCC report numbers these paras ten higher than the judgment as printed (56 to 66, 55 to 65). Para 21.1.1 of Jaskaran records that Mihir Rajesh Shah is prospective. The point is accurate but stopped at 'free to go', which could mislead a protester into thinking release ends the matter. Para 55 lets the police apply for remand or custody again after release, with reasons, once the written grounds are given and the delay is explained, and Jaskaran para 24 confirms that route. A sentence saying so is added, and para 55 is added to the quote.

fix.point: The Supreme Court has held that a person arrested for any offence, under any law including the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, must be given the grounds of arrest in writing, in a language they understand. If the officer cannot give them in writing at the time of arrest or soon after, the grounds must be told to the person orally. They must then be given in writing within a reasonable time, and at least two hours before the person is produced before the magistrate for remand. If this is not done, the arrest and the remand that follows are illegal and the person is free to go. The police may then ask the magistrate for custody again, giving their reasons, but only after giving the grounds in writing and explaining why they were not given in time. The Court said this procedure governs arrests from its judgment of 6 November 2025 onwards.
fix.quote: 55. It goes without saying that if the abovesaid schedule for supplying the grounds of arrest in writing is not adhered to, the arrest will be rendered illegal entitling the release of the arrestee. On such release, an application for remand or custody, if required, will be moved along with the reasons and necessity for the same, after the supply of the grounds of arrest in writing setting forth the explanation for non-supply thereof within the above stipulated schedule. 56. In conclusion, it is held that: i) The constitutional mandate of informing the arrestee the grounds of arrest is mandatory in all offences under all statutes including offences under IPC 1860 (now BNS 2023); ii) The grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to the arrestee in the language he/she understands; iii) In case(s) where, the arresting officer/person is unable to communicate the grounds of arrest in writing on or soon after arrest, it be so done orally. The said grounds be communicated in writing within a reasonable time and in any case at least two hours prior to production of the arrestee for remand proceedings before the magistrate. iv) In case of non-compliance of the above, the arrest and subsequent remand would be rendered illegal and the person will be at liberty to be set free. ... 58. ... The ends of fairness and legal discipline therefore demand that this procedure as affirmed above shall govern arrests henceforth.
fix.law: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra, Supreme Court (B.R. Gavai CJI and Augustine George Masih J.), 6 November 2025, Criminal Appeal No. 2195 of 2025, (2026) 1 SCC 500; paras 55, 56 and 58 in the judgment's own numbering as printed and shown on Indian Kanoon (paras 65, 66 and 68 in the SCC report, as Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, 21 September 2026, para 24, cites them)

fix.point: No one accused of an offence can be forced to be a witness against themselves. A person the police question during an investigation must answer truthfully the questions about the case. The law excuses that person from answering questions whose answers would tend to expose them to a criminal charge, a penalty or forfeiture.

topic: 3. Force must be minimal and proportionate
note: Opened dl/ik_139222628.txt (Anita Thakur v. Govt. of J&K, 12 August 2016, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 118 of 2007, Sikri J. author, with R.K. Agrawal J.). The para 12 sentences are verbatim (footnote marker 2 dropped, 'subsidised' as in the source), and para 12 is the judgment's own numbering. Two changes. First, the Court states the necessity, minimum and proportionality rule as what 'police manual and even international covenants' mandate, so the point now says the Court noted it from those documents. Second, para 13 opens 'In those cases where assembly is peaceful, use of police force is not warranted at all', with reasonable force justified only once a crowd turns violent. Leaving that out would mislead a protester at a peaceful assembly, so it is added to the point, the quote and the citation.

fix.point: The Supreme Court has said that police force is not warranted at all against a peaceful assembly. Where a crowd turns violent, reasonable force may be justified. The Court noted that police manuals and international covenants require force to be used only when it is absolutely necessary. When force is used, it should be the minimum needed and in proportion to the situation. It should stop as soon as the danger to life and property has passed.
fix.quote: 12. ... There are various documents in the form of police manual and even international covenants proscribing use of unnecessary force and mandating that force should only be used when it is absolutely necessary. Even when used, it should be minimum and proportional to the situation and its use to be discontinued as soon as the danger to life and property subsidised. 13. In those cases where assembly is peaceful, use of police force is not warranted at all. However, in those situations where crowd or assembly becomes violent it may necessitate and justify using reasonable police force.
fix.law: Anita Thakur v. Govt. of J&K, Supreme Court (A.K. Sikri and R.K. Agrawal JJ.), 12 August 2016, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 118 of 2007, paras 12 and 13 (the judgment's own numbering, which Indian Kanoon shows)

topic: 8. Assault or force to deter a public servant (s.132 BNS)
note: BNS section 132 checked in src/bns.txt, verbatim (replaces IPC 353). The First Schedule row for 132 in src/bnss.txt joins to the quoted text, cognizable and non-bailable, triable by any Magistrate. The point was accurate, but 'non-bailable' alone is commonly read as 'no bail', which would mislead a protester. BNSS section 480(1), opened in src/bnss.txt, says a person arrested or detained without warrant for a non-bailable offence 'may be released on bail', subject to conditions. A sentence saying so is added, with section 480(1) in the law and quote.

fix.point: Assaulting or using criminal force on a public servant who is carrying out their duty, or to stop them doing it, or because of something they did lawfully in that duty, is punishable with up to two years in prison, a fine, or both. The offence is cognizable and non-bailable. A person accused of a non-bailable offence may still be released on bail, but has no right to it, and the police officer or court decides.
fix.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 132 (replaces IPC section 353); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 132; BNSS section 480(1)
fix.quote: BNS 132: "Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person being a public servant in the execution of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by such person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both."
